title: The Bird That Hammers All Day
blurb: The bird that drills into trees twenty times a second, catches grubs with a tongue that wraps around its own skull, and builds homes for half the forest.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: This is a woodpecker. It sits on the side of a tree. It holds on with its feet. It leans back on its stiff tail. Then it hammers. Tap tap tap tap. The tree is hard, but its beak is harder. The woodpecker is looking for bugs under the bark. It has a long, sticky tongue. The tongue reaches in and pulls the bug out. Tap tap tap.

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Builds Doors
blocks.text: A woodpecker does not build its nest in a branch. It builds it inside the tree. First it picks a dead trunk with soft wood. Then it hammers a round hole and digs out a room. This takes many days. The wood chips fall to the ground like snow. When the chicks grow up, the family flies away and leaves the hole behind. The hole does not go to waste. Owls move in. Squirrels move in. Bluebirds and ducks and bats move in. None of them can cut a hole of their own. They wait for a woodpecker to do the work first.

wood chips
owls, squirrels, bluebirds, ducks and bats

blocks.prompt: The Tongue That Goes Around the Skull
blocks.text: A woodpecker's beak is a chisel. That part is easy to see. The stranger tool is hidden inside its head. A woodpecker's tongue is far too long to fit in its mouth, so the tongue keeps going. It slides back past the throat, splits in two, wraps up and around the back of the skull, over the top of the head, and ends near the base of the beak. Some woodpeckers can stick that tongue out three times the length of their beak. The tip is not smooth. It carries tiny barbs that face backward, like the hooks on a fish spear, and it is coated in sticky spit. When a woodpecker hammers a hole into rotten wood, it is not eating the wood. It is opening a door. Beetle grubs live in tunnels under the bark. The bird pushes its tongue down a tunnel, feels around a corner, hooks the grub, and pulls it out whole. The hole took a minute. The tongue takes a second.

answers: it wraps around the back and top of its skull
tiny backward barbs and sticky spit
to open a door to the grub tunnels under the bark
(inference: backward hooks stop the grub sliding off as the tongue pulls back)

4.title: The Bird That Hammers All Day
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Bird That Hammers All Day

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Two toes point forward, two point back
Stiff tail feathers work as a third leg
The beak grows back as it wears down
A see-through eyelid closes before each strike
Acorn woodpeckers store acorns in one tree
There are about 240 species worldwide

blocks.prompt: Built to Hit Things
blocks.text: Imagine trying to hammer a nail while hanging onto a wall. That is the woodpecker's whole job, and its body is built for it from the toes up. Start with the feet. Most birds have three toes forward and one back, which is good for gripping a branch from above. A woodpecker has two toes forward and two back, which turns its foot into a pair of pincers that grip bark from the side. Next comes the tail. A woodpecker's tail feathers are unusually stiff, with thickened shafts, so the bird can press them against the trunk and use the tail as a third leg. Feet and tail together make a tripod. The bird is not hanging on. It is braced. Then the beak. It is a chisel, and it wears down as it works, but it also grows continuously from the base, so it sharpens itself. Around the nostrils grow small bristly feathers that filter out the sawdust. A fraction of a second before every strike, a thin extra eyelid called the nictitating membrane sweeps across the eye. It keeps chips out, and it holds the eyeball firmly in place. Not every woodpecker uses the kit the same way. The acorn woodpecker of the western United States drills thousands of shallow holes in a single dead tree and jams one acorn into each. A well used storage tree can hold fifty thousand acorns, and a family of birds will defend it for generations. The sapsucker drills neat rows of small wells and returns later to drink the sap that leaks out, along with the insects the sap has trapped. Every one of those features solves a problem created by the one job the bird refuses to give up.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Foraging taps and drumming are different sounds
Drumming claims territory and calls a mate
Birds drum on gutters and signs because metal is loud
Most woodpeckers cannot sing
Old nest holes house owls, bats and squirrels
Biologists call them a keystone species

blocks.prompt: The Sound Is the Point
blocks.text: There are two kinds of woodpecker noise, and they are not the same thing at all. The first is foraging. It is uneven and businesslike: a few taps, a pause, a chip of bark flicked away, a few more taps. The bird is working. It is listening and feeling for the hollow tunnels that beetle grubs leave under the bark, and when it finds one it opens the wood and reaches in with its long barbed tongue. The second kind is drumming, and it has nothing to do with food. A drum is a fast, even burst of blows delivered on whatever surface will carry the sound farthest. That last part is the key. The woodpecker is not choosing good wood. It is choosing a loud object. Birds have been recorded drumming on hollow limbs, on metal gutters, on chimney flashing, on street signs and on satellite dishes, because a resonant metal surface broadcasts a claim across a far wider area than soft wood ever could. Most songbirds sing. Woodpeckers mostly cannot. So drumming does the work that song does for a robin: it announces who owns this patch of forest, and it advertises for a mate. The pattern carries real information. Species differ in the speed of the roll, its length, and whether it slows at the end, and a listening bird can tell a rival of its own kind from a harmless neighbor of another. There is a third thing woodpeckers do, and they do it without meaning to. Every pair excavates a fresh nest hole, and most holes are used once and then abandoned. Across a forest, that adds up to a standing supply of ready made cavities. Chickadees, bluebirds, wrens, kestrels, screech owls, flying squirrels and several kinds of bat all need holes, and none of them can cut one. Biologists call an animal like this a keystone species: pull it out and a whole community of others loses its housing. The hammering that sounds like damage is, for a great many neighbors, construction.

6.title: The Bird That Hammers All Day
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Bird That Hammers All Day

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Up to 20 strikes per second, thousands per day
Each impact stops the head in about a millisecond
The spongy bone and looping tongue bone were the old explanation
High speed film in 2022 found no cushioning at all
A woodpecker brain weighs about two grams
A human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms

blocks.prompt: The Shock Absorber That Was Never There
blocks.text: For most of a century, the woodpecker came with a tidy explanation attached to it, and the explanation was wrong. The problem it tried to solve is real. A woodpecker strikes wood up to twenty times a second and may land thousands of blows in a day. Each impact stops its head in about a thousandth of a second, at decelerations many times greater than the ones that concuss a football player. A bird doing this should be knocked senseless by breakfast. So biologists went looking for the cushion, and they found candidates everywhere. Part of the skull is built of spongy bone. The upper and lower halves of the beak are slightly different lengths. The long hyoid bone that carries the tongue loops all the way around the braincase like a seatbelt. Each of these was a reasonable guess. Together they hardened into a fact: the woodpecker's head is a shock absorber. The claim traveled into textbooks, onto museum labels, and through the patent applications of helmet designers. In 2022 a team led by the biomechanist Sam Van Wassenbergh decided to actually watch. They filmed three species with high speed cameras and tracked the eye and the tip of the beak separately, frame by frame. If the skull were absorbing shock, the beak would stop first while the braincase kept traveling a little, compressing something in between. That is not what the footage showed. Beak and braincase decelerated together, as one stiff object. There was no measurable cushion. The head is not a shock absorber. It is a hammer. Then the researchers pointed out why that should have been obvious. A shock absorber's job is to convert motion into wasted heat. A woodpecker that cushioned its own blows would be throwing away the energy it swings for, and every bit of softness in the skull would mean more pecks to open the same hole. Natural selection had a choice between protecting the brain and drilling the tree, and it chose the tree. Which leaves the original question standing. If nothing is cushioned, why is the bird fine? The answer is size, and it disappoints only because we expected something cleverer. A human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms. A woodpecker's weighs about two grams. Concussion is not caused by deceleration alone. It is caused by the force a brain's own mass drives into the inside of its own skull. Shrink the brain and that force shrinks with it, while the bone holding it barely gets weaker. A brain that small, pressed snugly against bone with almost no fluid to slosh in, and stopped inside a millisecond, never reaches the pressure that injures a large one. The researchers ran the numbers and put the woodpecker comfortably below the threshold where a larger brain would be damaged. It is not armored. It is simply too small to hurt itself. There is a lesson buried in this, and it is not about birds. The shock absorber story survived for decades because it was elegant, because it explained a genuine puzzle, and because nobody filmed the animal to check. It also cost something real: helmet engineers spent years copying an anatomy that was never doing the job they believed it was doing. The woodpecker was never solving the problem we had assigned it. It was solving a different one, and it was solving it by being small.

(it turns at There is a lesson buried in this, and it is not about birds; the target is how an elegant unchecked explanation persists and misleads; earned by the textbook, museum and helmet-patent evidence given earlier)
